paras: The threatened lynching of George Mitchell took place on Sunday afternoon, March 18, 1888, near the Virginia end of the Aqueduct bridge in Alexandria County, Virginia, when a large crowd threatened to lynch Mitchell, a Black county constable, after he shot Roger Fields, a young white man from Washington. Mitchell was hidden in a nearby stable guarded by a bulldog and later escaped, and no one was reported hurt by the crowd. Washington, Alexandria and Richmond papers disagreed over whether Mitchell had provoked the fight or fired in self-defense.

A county resident told the Alexandria Gazette that since the free Aqueduct bridge opened, "great crowds" from Washington and Georgetown crossed to the Virginia side on Sundays, some of them gambling and boisterous. Mitchell was described as a constable of Alexandria County, and the Richmond Dispatch called him "a village constable" and placed the affair at Rosslyn.

Accounts of the encounter that led to the shooting differ. In the version Fields gave a Star reporter, two Black men offered him and a companion, "Bud" Roland, a game of cards, and after a white boy said the cards had been taken from him that morning, the constable grabbed for them and seized Roland by the collar. Fields said that when he interfered he was held by the second man, drew a small penknife and threatened to cut him, and was shot in the left side. The Washington Critic and the National Republican instead reported that Mitchell had invited Rowland to play, that a friend of Mitchell's came up with a club during the scuffle, and that Mitchell fired when Fields went to his friend's aid.

A county resident and Mitchell himself told a different story. In their version Mitchell had taken the cards from young men gambling, "telling them it was against the law," and the men returned with others and assaulted him with a knife and what he took for brass knuckles before he fired. The Dispatch's Alexandria correspondent described the returning party as "principally toughs and blacklegs that infest there on Sundays" and said Mitchell fired when surrounded and threatened by Fields with a knife.

After the shooting, according to the Critic, Mitchell "was threatened with lynching by the large crowd present." He was taken to the stable of John Clark, who locked him in and turned a bulldog loose "to keep off intruders." The Dispatch said it was "with the greatest difficulty" that Mitchell was gotten to the stable, where he was guarded until night. The county resident said the crowd "attempted to lynch the constable" but dispersed when help came, and the Gazette added that Mitchell afterwards escaped. Fields was taken to Georgetown, where Dr. Suter extracted the ball from a wound the Gazette called slight and the Critic "serious but not dangerous."

The Gazette reported that the next county grand jury was expected to investigate, and the Star's Alexandria correspondent wrote that it would hear witnesses when it met on the fourth Monday of May. No report of the grand jury's action, a charge against Mitchell, or arrests in the crowd was found.

The Washington Critic headed its report "A Murderous Assault" and gave the lynching threat a single sentence, while the National Republican, under "Shot by a Constable," said only that "Mitchell was arrested by the citizens." The Evening Star printed Fields' version from an interview, calling Mitchell "a colored constable" and at one point "the negro," and said the men escaped "followed by a large and angry crowd" without mentioning lynching.

Reports from the Virginia side leaned toward the constable. The Alexandria Gazette set Fields' account, in wording close to the Star's, beside a county resident's defense of Mitchell, and the Richmond Dispatch's special telegram blamed "toughs and blacklegs" and called the crowd "the mob." The Star's Alexandria column of March 21 reported Mitchell's claim of self-defense, naming him "Robert Mitchell."

Reports differ on what became of Mitchell: the National Republican said citizens arrested him, the Star that he escaped with a crowd behind him, and the Gazette that he hid in a stable and later escaped. Most reports name him George, but the Star's Alexandria column calls him Robert.

accounts.label: Fields' account
accounts.gist: Two Black men offered cards; the constable grabbed Roland by the collar, the other man seized Fields, and when Fields drew a penknife and threatened to cut him, his captor shot him. The men then escaped with a large, angry crowd following.

accounts.label: Washington report (Critic, National Republican)
accounts.gist: Mitchell invited Rowland to play cards; a friend of Mitchell came with a club, and Mitchell shot Fields as he went to Rowland's aid. The Critic says the crowd threatened to lynch Mitchell; the Republican says citizens arrested him.

accounts.label: County resident's account
accounts.gist: Mitchell took cards from gamblers as unlawful; they returned with others and assaulted him with a knife and apparent brass knuckles, and he shot one. The crowd attempted to lynch him but dispersed when help came.

accounts.label: Constable's claim
accounts.gist: Mitchell said the young men he had taken the cards from came back with others and assaulted him, and he fired in self-defense.

accounts.label: Richmond Dispatch Alexandria telegram
accounts.gist: Boys whose game Mitchell interrupted brought 'toughs and blacklegs' back to thrash him; surrounded and threatened by Fields with a knife, he fired; the mob threatened lynching, and he was gotten to a stable with great difficulty and guarded by bulldogs until night.

framing.detail: The Critic headed it 'A Murderous Assault' by Mitchell but reported the lynching threat plainly as an aftermath.
The Evening Star printed Fields' interview, calling Mitchell 'a colored constable' and once 'the negro', and omitted any lynching threat.
The Alexandria Gazette printed Fields' version and a county resident's defense of the constable side by side, the latter saying the crowd 'attempted to lynch' him.
The National Republican's 'Shot by a Constable' said only that citizens arrested Mitchell.
The Richmond Dispatch blamed 'toughs and blacklegs that infest there on Sundays' and called the crowd 'the mob'.
